candidate.answerReason: Under the standard independent-toss model, the even and odd probabilities sum to 1 and differ by \((-1/3)^{50}=3^{-50}\). The resulting even probability agrees with choice D.

methods.label: Track even and odd probabilities
methods.explanation:
Use the usual model of independent tosses, each with heads probability \(2/3\). Only whether the current number of heads is even or odd matters: a tail preserves this status, while a head switches it.

Let \(E_n\) and \(O_n\) be the probabilities of an even and an odd number of heads after \(n\) tosses. Initially, \(E_0=1\) and \(O_0=0\), because zero is even. For \(0\le n<50\), independence gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_{n+1}&=\frac13E_n+\frac23O_n,\\
O_{n+1}&=\frac13O_n+\frac23E_n.
\end{aligned}
\]
For example, an even count results from an even count followed by a tail, or an odd count followed by a head. These possibilities are disjoint.

Subtracting the equations is useful because the same difference reappears:
\[
E_{n+1}-O_{n+1}=-\frac13(E_n-O_n).
\]
Starting with \(E_0-O_0=1\), each toss multiplies the difference by \(-1/3\). Thus
\[
E_{50}-O_{50}=\left(-\frac13\right)^{50}=\frac1{3^{50}}.
\]
Every count is either even or odd, so \(E_{50}+O_{50}=1\). Adding these last two equations gives
\[
E_{50}=\frac12\left(1+\frac1{3^{50}}\right).
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

methods.label: Cancel the odd binomial terms
methods.explanation:
Assume independent tosses, and write \(p=2/3\) for the heads probability and \(q=1/3\) for the tails probability. For exactly \(k\) heads, there are \(\binom{50}{k}\) choices of head positions. Each choice describes a distinct sequence with probability \(p^kq^{50-k}\). Therefore the desired probability is the sum of these terms for \(k=0,2,4,\ldots,50\).

The binomial theorem lets us collect all those even terms without calculating them separately. In the expansions of \((q+p)^{50}\) and \((q-p)^{50}\), the terms containing an odd power of \(p\) have opposite signs, while those containing an even power have the same sign. Adding the expansions cancels the odd terms and doubles precisely the desired terms. Hence the probability is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{(q+p)^{50}+(q-p)^{50}}2
&=\frac{1+(-1/3)^{50}}2\\
&=\frac12\left(1+\frac1{3^{50}}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
The sum includes both zero heads and fifty heads, so all even possibilities are covered. The answer is \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
